speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The time for questions and comments is over. The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) has the floor.

Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, I know other Members want to speak and our time is limited, so I will do something I usually do not do, stay fairly close to my notes.
I listened with a great deal of interest to my friend, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who always speaks with eloquence and passion. I agree with much of what he said. I am not going to touch on some of the things I fully agree with, especially what he said about the North. However,
I want to deal with some of the other items that he mentioned.
This is either the beauty, the challenge or the curse of this debate. In listening to his logic in interpreting the Meech Lake Accord I am almost reaffirmed in my concern about some of the very things he sees so positively, but which I think create real problems. He talks quite rightly about the Machiavellian politics going on in the other Chamber by that muse from Lake Ainslie in Nova Scotia, MacEachen Incorporated. He has come out of his cave of hibernation and is trying to impose himself in the parliamentary process by playing monopoly with the concerns of the citizens of this country.
I said, along with Stanley Knowles, many years ago that I am for abolition of the Senate. One of my first essays in political science dealt with the reform of the Senate. However, what I cannot accept from my hon. friend who just spoke so well is that he laments the hacks, flacks, and all the political patronage in that Chamber down the hall, yet does not raise any questions about how the new method works. There is still going to be appointments of hacks, flacks, and good people, but instead of being appointed only by a Prime Minister after consultation, the appointments will now come from a list provided by the provinces. The form has not been changed.
If my hon. friend, who has been around here for a few years, along with some Premiers who are a little newer to the political game, really believes, given the unanimity rule for amending federal institutions, that there is a snowball's chance in that place down below of making any fundamental reform to the Senate, he is wrong. Triple E goes out the window. Instead of

June 12, 1987
Constitutional Accord
equal, effective and elected, it will be echo chamber, eternal, and ineffective. It is as dead as a dodo bird. Senate reform is as dead as the dinosaurs in Drumheller. Yet my friend waxes eloquently and quite passionately about what is going on down there and how they are becoming very partisan in their deliberations on this very fundamental document.
Quite frankly, I am not going to be partisan today because this document cuts across Party lines and there is real concern in all Parties about the Meech Lake Accord. I agree that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) brought a tremendous feeling of national reconciliation to this country after the election of 1984. We do not have the confrontation we had before. He deserves a lot of credit for getting the 10 Premiers around the table and coming up with an agreement. That is very rare. Yet we cannot be completely blind to the way some people interpret the implications of that agreement. We can all have visions of national reconciliation but we have to know if this constitutional document is going to stand the test of time; not when everyone is feeling very good and very co-operative but when there is stress and strain on the federation, as there is from time to time.
Do not bring the dragon of Pierre Trudeau out and say that is the man of yesterday. He was Prime Minister for 16 or 18 years, and in that sense he is the past, but some of the questions, if not the way he raised them, are very legitimate. I am glad Canadians are going to have a chance to assess those questions now that we have this motion to send the matter to a joint committee. I will not get into that, but I compliment my House Leader for doing that. They will have their chance if the committee gets input from the public, and hopefully the provincial legislatures will have their public input as well.
The amendment suggested by my friend from Yorkton- Melville is interesting and constructive, but the fact is we have to decide whether it is co-operative federalism or whether it is going to be fractured federalism. I am going to refer to something which is central to that question, and that is the spending power. Before I do I want to read into the record a letter 1 wrote to my Prime Minister on May 12. The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) had spoken out, but this was before Mr. Trudeau spoke out. I talked about vision and my basic instinctive concern about what Meech Lake would do. It reads:
My Dear Prime Minister,
Notwithstanding your eloquent and sensitive speech yesterday, it is with regret and after much wrenching introspection that I am duty bound to inform you that in all conscience I cannot agree to the Meech Lake Accord. 1 sincerely believe that in the laudable desire to get Quebec "in", we are so fundamentally changing the future character of Canada that the "one Canada" I believe in will become too loose a Confederation with the Federal Government no longer being first among equals but merely one among equals.
I am not too disturbed about Quebec's justified claim of being a "distinct society"-but with the opting out process along with compensation, there is no doubt in my mind that in time, and soon, there will be a de facto "deux nations", let alone sovereignty-association status in that Province. Accordingly, I can appreciate why the Bourassa position has been positively received in Quebec, while unfortunately, and dangerously, in a political sense, the rest of Canada is so numb (and bored) over the constitutional process, that the
fundamental implications of nation building at Meech Lake are not receiving the proper attention they deserve.
Therefore, in my view, a one day debate in the House, while commendable, is not sufficient. However, I appreciate that the fine print of the necessary legislation will provide an opportunity for a further debate of the principles of the Accord. Nevertheless, recognizing the reality of the parliamentary and political process and the limitation of time for government business, I feel these principles should be debated now-and surely if these suggested constitutional changes are to stand the test of time, then they should now be able to withstand public and parliamentary scrutiny.
At a minimum, a parliamentary committee of both Houses should be given an opportunity to seek and hear the public's view.
This would provide a vehicle for meaningful public input on the principles of the Accord to assess whether the opting out clause might adversely affect the leadership role of the federal Government let alone the provincial veto on national institutions which surely consigns Senate reform to the perpetual backwater of a constitutional strait-jacket.
Furthermore, the institutionalizing of annual federal-provincial conferences on the Constitution and the economy, with possibly the real agreements being made (necessarily) behind closed doors, will surely render the parliamentary process somewhat redundant and hence the House of Commons, for at least the important national issues, will become a mere rubber stamp.
1 have no doubt, Mr. Prime Minister, of the intensity and passion of our Francophone colleagues in all Parties with respect to their support for the Accord.
I recall when Premier Bourassa said that Quebec could not agree with the Victoria Amending Formula, he eloquently emphasized that his position was not anti-Canada but pro-Quebec. Likewise, I am not anti-Quebec but pro-Canada and Mr. Prime Minister, 1 hold my position with as much passion and intensity as do our Francophone colleagues.
The reason I read the letter was to indicate that that was my instinct at a time long before others who had more responsibility in running the country spoke out.
Why is there such concern in terms of the powers of the federal Government? 1 will not repeat what 1 said about the Senate. However, we can forget about reform in the Senate and Triple E. Anyone who thinks that there will be fundamental reform of the unanimity rule is whistling Dixie.
I should like to refer to the American experience. They are celebrating the two hundredth anniversary of their Constitution. They started with 13 little States, and they had an amending formula which required unanimity. The whole system bogged down in that more simple day. They had to reframe their Constitution and provide the amending formula which they now have where there is some flexibility.
It is ironic that we took so many years-a hundred or so-to get our Constitution back into the country where it properly should be. It had an amending formula and then, almost out of the blue-although I admit that there was a year-long negotiation behind closed doors-we are to put federal institutions into a constitutional strait-jacket from which they will never be changed.
In terms of the spending power, I should like to say that this is a very complex, complicated situation. I agree with the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount that perhaps some of these matters should be considered by
June 12, 1987

stated case in the Supreme Court to get some judicial direction before we put the Constitution into constitutional stone.
This matter is different from the bilateral agreements with provinces. The Cullen-Coutre immigration agreement is a bilateral agreement between Quebec and Canada on immigration. There are many bilateral agreements between the federal Government and the provinces from time to time, which are not frozen in constitutional stone.
The problem with the Meech Lake Accord is that we are taking some of those de facto, ad hoc bilateral situations which require flexibility from time to time and we are putting them into a Constitution which is much more difficult to change.
Let us look at the spending power. The spending power is tremendously different. I know there are different types of arrangements now in the different social plans in the country and that each province must have some variation. However, that is much better than the present document which we are considering. Those who have been seduced by the semantic changes which occurred in a 20-hour session in the Langevin Building illustrate the danger of our moving too fast down the constitutional road without some judicial assessment of the real interpretation.
I can understand; I have an Indian community in my riding. They were here for the constitutional debate on aboriginal rights. Talk about second-class Canadians which members of the NDP mention in rhetoric yet do nothing about in reality!
What if you were one of the aboriginals, Madam Speaker, who came to Ottawa several months ago and found the constitutional conference floundering because the participants would not or could not define aboriginal self-government or aboriginal rights? It is a legitimate question; it is a very difficult thing to define. However, that conference failed because they could not define it. Yet, you got something else- a "distinctive society" with opting out features with compensation. Somehow the Premier of Ontario admitted in Queen's Park that the courts would define that. Don't you think you would have been a little hard done by? Don't you think that that is one of the reasons there is some irritation and quite proper irritation?
We are prepared to leave things to the court on one hand- the Meech Lake Accord. However, on other matters which affect people and their rights, we shy away from them and say that we cannot come to an agreement. I tell you, Madam Speaker, that is hypocrisy of the highest order.
Let me refer to something else which is not on record. Quite frankly, I think the press have been lazy laggards in really assessing the implications of the Accord, the rat-pack journalism which goes on around here. They get mesmerized by Trudeau and they do not do their homework.
1 will read another document into the record. It is only one of many which I have. I hope someone follows through on it, so that when we get to the committee, those who appear before the committee to give evidence can be examined.
Constitutional Accord
I should like to quote from a Canadian Press story dated May 11,	1983 concerning the Conservative leadership
campaign. It is one of the softest ones. There are others which have much more pejorative terms about what candidates were saying about each other and about the positions of their fellow colleagues running in the race to be leader of my Party. It is part of the confusion.
Four years ago, very responsible, competent, conscientious, serious politicians had something to say about the opting out formula. There is a complete change today. Surely they must come before the committee to be examined on why it was so bad four years ago and is most acceptable today.
I will read one of many clippings; I am not going to bore you, Madam Speaker. The May 11, 1983, CP story reads as follows:
Joe Clark is playing "fast and loose with the historical truth" when he claims his proposed constitutional concession to Quebec is official Progressive Conservative policy, says leadership candidate David Crombie.
Crombie says the proposal, supported by the Tories during the 1981 constitutional debate and now opposed by all leadership candidates but Clark, was merely a last minute political ploy designed to embarrass the Government by attracting support from Quebec Liberal Senators.
The Tories argued then-as Clark does now-that up to three provinces should get full financial compensation if they opt out of a constitutional change that transfers provincial powers to Ottawa.
Crombie, a member of the all-Party constitution committee, said he and others opposed the idea but voted for the unsuccessful Tory amendment because of pressure from Clark to show caucus solidarity.
Jake Epp, the top Tory constitutional spokesman at the time, says Crombie is rewriting history to justify why he, John Crosbie and Michael Wilson have changed their minds on the issue.
"Obviously it is Party policy-caucus voted for it", Epp said Wednesday. "I don't understand the flip-flopping".
The complicated issue of fiscal compensation may now be, as Crosbie says, "a pretty academic question."
Yet it reflects a tougher Tory attitude toward Quebec's demands and has added some weird twists to the leadership race:
-Clark was booed at a Toronto debate, accused of selling out to separatists and criticized by Anglophone editorialists for defending a position held in 1981 first by eight Premiers and then by his caucus.
-In the heat of the race, three former cabinet Ministers have suddenly revealed a change of mind. Crombie admits he voted for something he didn't believe in. Crosbie was surprised when reminded he once voted for it. Wilson confused compensation with another issue during the Toronto debate .. . Brian Mulroney, who has also savaged Clark's position, says he has his own nine-point constitutional plan but aides can't produce a copy or say exactly what it is ...
ironically, Clark's opponents have landed squarely in the camp of their chief enemy, Prime Minister Trudeau, who says fiscal compensation would amount to "incremental separatism."
Trudeau said in an interview published last weekend: "I note with a bit of amusement that the people who supported him (Clark) then and booed the Government. .. now are taking our side against Mr. Clark."
Clark argues his position is consistent with a more decentralized view of federalism and aids all provinces, not just Quebec.
Crosbie, Crombie and Wilson say they have reassessed their position.
This is another CP story of May 4 which ties in with what I
have just read:

June 12, 1987
Constitutional Accord
Conservative Leadership candidate Brian Mulroney accused the Party Quebecois government Tuesday of preventing Quebec from reaching a constitutional understanding with the rest of Canada.
This is a compliment to the Prime Minister about more or less what happened, but it does not really answer the question about physical compensation. It continues:
"Get rid of the PQ, and as Prime Minister of Canada, I'd negotiate constitutional peace with the people of Quebec just like that," Mulroney said while visiting Tories in northeastern Quebec.
He said it is "practically impossible" to improve relations between Quebec and Ottawa as long as the PQ is in power.
Mulroney has been criticizing his leadership rival Joe Clark for playing into the hands of the PQ by promising to insert in the Constitution a formula allowing the provinces to opt out of amendments with financial compensation.
The Montreal businessman has refused to specify his own views on Quebec's constitutional discontents, saying it would be bad strategy for a future Prime Minister to tip his bargaining hand to Premier Rene Levesque.
Mulroney announced a nine-point "formula for rekindling the kind of alliance between Canadians which Sir John A. MacDonald spoke of more than 100 years ago."
I took the time to read that, Madam Speaker, because that just shows you the difficulty and the complexity of this opting out formula. Does it strengthen Canada or does it make a French Canada?
My friend from Yorkton-Melville can quote Tommy Douglas. Tommy Douglas who started medicare in Saskatchewan never would have had medicare as a national program if this opting out compensation formula were in place. We all know the history.
Premier Robarts of Ontario was dragged into the plan because Prime Minister Pearson said, "you will have four criteria and if you get four criteria you will be part of medicare. If you don't get into the plan, we will test you anyway". That is really political blackmail in provincial jurisdiction, admittedly, but that is what got the medicare plan launched. It would not have happened, in my submission, if we had the present opting out compensation formula that is in the Meech Lake Accord.
I think you are indicating that my time is almost up, Madam Speaker. I will leave the Accord but I would like to touch on one other thing which reflects on Parliament and which bothers me. I do believe in Parliament. I understand there is a de facto form of Government, that is, federal-provincial conferences. They have become very important. To institutionalize them into the Constitution on a yearly basis really makes this place rather redundant. Put a Member on the government side in my position, something that I have nothing to do with, understandably, because I was not there in the negotiations, yet there is a hosanna and a euphoria about an agreement because everyone comes together. Yet if I voice objections to what I have been no party to and on which I never ran an election, I become, in effect, an implied traitor to the cause.
I agree completely with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), and, I hope, my House Leader, for whom I have the highest respect who made a light remark
about me, about my seniority. Perhaps my seniority will be the only thing I will have left when I sit down.
Oh, oh!

These things will come on a yearly basis. We have to change the rules, as the Hon. Member for Windsor West said, so there can be some provision to trigger a debate, such as there is in Manitoba, when constitutional accords are made.
In conclusion, and this is a conclusion, I admit, this stuff all started in recent times with Premier Robarts calling Premiers together for the Confederation Conference of Tomorrow in Toronto in 1967. I just want to say one thing, something that I will never forget because I was then a brand new Member. I would not have even suggested participating in any meaningful debate but it never really came on to the floor of the House. The Attorney General of Ontario, Arthur Wishert, said, in defining the problems of entrenching rights and having a written Constitution, that in the civil law the only rights you have are what is written down, whereas in the unwritten common law they are wide open unless they are taken away.
Just to divorce myself from Pierre Trudeau, I say we have the worst of both worlds unless there are some meaningful amendments to this matter. We have the Supreme Court of Canada de facto legislating on a Charter of Rights, which no one fully understands-that is arguable-it may be good or bad. Now with this Meech Lake Accord institutionalizing constitutional agreements and no one knowing what the Accord really means, we will have the Supreme Court again legislating, doing our work, telling us what we should have written, and I say that is the worst of both worlds.
I am so glad that we have at least got this thing launched in a committee. I really do hope that Members from all sides over a period of time will have a chance to contribute. If we can spend days on capital punishment and days on the Patent Act and drugs, surely Members of Parliament should take the responsibility and in the right place and at the right time speak out on this-whichever way they feel-because constitutions, as someone said earlier, are for people, not just for the leaders of the land.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) that now that he has sat down he has his seniority but he also has his self-respect, and that is terribly important.
My question arises out of his comments that the courts will tell us what we have done. He referred, I think, to a comment of Premier Peterson and he also referred to the over-all thrust of the Accord which will place even greater legislative power, if you like, in the hands of the courts.
I am not sure if the Hon. Member was here earlier when I mentioned that I had written to the Premiers and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and suggested that a number of the ambiguities in this Accord could be cleared up by reference cases, provincially and federally. Would he comment on that
June 12, 1987

as an appropriate procedure, given that some of these issues, not some of the fundamental ones which he raises, such as the institutionalization of First Ministers' conferences-we all know where that could lead, as he has pointed out-but some of the ambiguities in specific sections, whether it be on spending power, distinct society versus distinct identity, or the issue of whether that provision in turn overrides the Charter and so on, it seems to me, Madam Speaker, not only could be but should be put to the courts so they can tell us now, when we look at this resolution and debate it in the House, what those provisions actually mean.
Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member was momentarily out of the House. I did comment on that and I thought it was a good idea.

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment on the speech of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). He had a lot of concerns and believed that there are many questions regarding this Accord. I believe those are legitimate concerns and 1 share some of them. I hope, as a result of the committee process, that we will have a number of people not only addressing those concerns but addressing a number of others which many people across the country have as to the exact wording and meaning of the Accord.
When the Member says that this Accord weakens Confederation-and that is the implication he left-he should also recognize that the constitutional package of 1981, for which 1 believe he voted, also was a vague package, a package going to the courts which enshrined a Charter of Rights the exact implications of which even at this stage many of us do not know when we passed it in those days. This is not something new. His Prime Minister and the Premiers did not do something new this year. This is an ongoing process and it will always be a problem when we deal with constitutional changes. The Member accepts and agrees with the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) that that is a valid position. He is probably quite sincere in his opinion, but he must admit that those are not the same reservations that he himself had in 1981.
The Hon. Member referred to the New Democratic Party and our position on aboriginal rights. He inferred from the motion we have before us, which the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) put forward, that we are concerned about the Yukon and the Northwest Territories being left out. He also somehow inferred that we are not concerned that aboriginal people were also left out. That can hardly be true. The Member has heard us speak on this issue. He knows that on Monday of this week the New Democratic Party had a motion calling for another First Ministers' meeting on aboriginal rights. In that same motion we again referred to the need to recognize the existing rights of the people from the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and the aboriginal people. That motion which was put to the House was not a motion of confidence in the Government. We explained that in the first speech that was made by a member
Constitutional Accord
of the NDP. The Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants voted against that amendment. I think there is a contradiction there, and before he criticizes us for putting forward these amendments on a consistent basis, twice this week, he should at least admit that we have been trying but sometimes he has not supported our efforts.

Madam Speaker, I was very brief in replying to the Hon. Member's first intervention and I appreciate the remarks of the Hon. Member in a sense. However, let us not kid ourselves and play games. I was in opposition for 18 years. We used to think up dream motions that we knew would be turned down.
The Hon. Member is correct. Because of the questions in the Meech Lake Accord over aboriginal rights and the north, 1 suppose, to be logical, I would vote against it, and a couple of Members did so. However, the Hon. Member knows as well as I do that that was a Supply motion. He may say that it is not a confidence motion, but the fact is that it dealt with one of the most integral parts of the whole parliamentary process, and that is Supply.
There is another rule that indicates that such a motion was not a motion of confidence, and the Hon. Member has said that it was not, but I have my interpretation. I used to sit on that side of the House and plot motions that would embarrass the Government. The Government would be caught between a rock and a hard place because the motion would be for motherhood. Yet the reality is that it is a vote of confidence.
I had no hesitation in voting with my Party on a confidence motion. While 1 may have some reservations about the interpretations of the Accord, I hope that the joint committee does resolve some of them and I hope that my fears are unfounded. That is a heck of a lot different from voting against a Government on a confidence motion.
I say to my friends in the NDP that I have the greatest respect for the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). He is one of the most active speakers in the House.
1 do not want to be too partisan because I hope that this matter can be debated in a political but not a partisan way. That is what I resent so much about the Senate.
When the Hon. Member said that he was a leopard that did not change his spots, I had a little dirty thought. I thought, yes, sometimes that fellow is pretty strong and perhaps has some spots. However, in this case, given the history of his Party with the Regina Manifesto, Woodsworth, Coldwell and Lewis, he is a tabby-cat. That Party is a tabby-cat. NDP used to mean "New Democratic Principle". Some of us thought it meant "No Damned Principles", but now it means "No Disturbing Polls". They want to ensure that they do not rock the boat and perhaps they will slip through.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) has spoken passionately about a Constitution that needs to reflect the essence of

June 12, 1987
Constitutional Accord
Canada and of Canadians. He has said that a Constitution needs to address the aspirations of the country's people and not necessarily of the country's political leaders. He also spoke very passionately about how the Accord treats and addresses the first citizens of Canada, the aboriginal people. I appreciated his passionate plea for bringing down to earth what a Constitution is supposed to be. In essence, a Constitution is supposed to define its country and its people.
Toward that end, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. Having spoken to the people, having recognized the aboriginal fact of Canada, and acknowledging the fact that there is both a French and an English heritage in Canada, would the Hon. Member be supportive of an amendment that would add in Clause 1 the fourth indisputable reality of Canada, which is its multicultural nature?
Multicultural Canadians have made contributions to Canada, not only in contemporary times but in fact in history. The aspirations of that sector of society for their children in years to come should be recognized. There is a belief in Canada that Canadians who are of neither French nor English origin have somehow been relegated to a second-class status. These people have been included in the Constitution as a footnote in Section 16. However, Clause 1 at the beginning of the Constitution basically sets out what Canada is. Would the Hon. Member support an inclusion of the concept of Canada being made up of four fundamental characters, the French, the English, the aboriginal and the multicultural people?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair would appreciate a short answer from the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan).

It is a very fundamental and important question, Madam Speaker, but my answer can be short.
Just as an aside to my friend from Yorkton-Melville who spoke of the Constitution and of Trudeau and the worst events let me say that the Constitution must cover all events and it must be for good times and for bad.
I think my hon. friend has just raised one of the real questions that must be resolved. 1 know what he is getting at in the abstract. I will wait and see what will be done through amendments.
I am a political realist and I think the Hon. Member is as well. When 10 Premiers and a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) put their signatures to a document, it will take a lot of public persuasion to ensure that these are the necessary changes to reflect the reality of Canada, which I think is what the Hon. Member has suggested that it is.

Madam Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), has put before us a very important matter that requires some comment. As you know, Madam Speaker, the people who will be appointed to the special joint committee to examine the Accord will have a very
noble and important task ahead of them. They will be examining an extremely important, significant and historical document.
What distresses me about the proposal of the Minister of Justice is that he has set out in the rules for this committee a deadline for reporting back to the House of September 14. 1 find that extremely difficult to understand and actually unacceptable.
The House of Commons can debate for over a year the question of capital punishment. It can debate for six months the question of pornography. It can debate for months and months the question of the cost of prescription drugs and medicine. Yet when it comes to this fundamental, basic document, the super-law of Canada, the Government has set a time limit of three months, including the summer months, for deliberation and examination of such a fundamental document. That I wish to raise in the strongest possible terms as being a ludicrous way of dealing with the Canadian Constitution.
A time limit puts undue and unnecessary pressure on members of the committee to report back to the House on a matter that is extremely difficult and which must be explained. Some of us have enormous difficulties understanding it, and I will mention that again in a few moments. As well, the public needs the time to absorb the issue.
I thought that a columnist here in Ottawa put it very well a few days ago when he wrote that the Accord can be examined not as a sacred text from Mount Sinai but as the flawed work of 11 politicians burning the midnight oil and jockeying for advantage, and that it can be held up to the light to check for cracks. I think that is a good way of describing the substance of this document. It needs a very thorough examination, and the time limit on that process is unacceptable.
As presently written, the Meech Lake Accord, as you must have noticed from Question Period, editorials and articles, raises many questions. I will deal with only a few of them. First, Clause 1 does not really reflect the composition of today's Canadian society. That matter was raised in Question Period by my colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), only a few minutes ago. The description of Canadian society in Clause 1 must definitely be amended in order to provide for recognition of the existence of Canadians whose language is neither English nor French but who are Canadian citizens and make daily substantial and phenomenal contributions to the fabric and substance of this society.
Second, and of equal importance, as has been raised by others, in particular the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), is the importance of recognizing, not as an afterthought at the end of the document but in Clause 1, the existence of the aboriginal peoples. I congratulate and salute my colleagues for having raised that so forcefully, intensively and repeatedly in the House of Commons in preceding days.
June 12, 1987

Therefore, it is absolutely necessary to deal with Clause (2)(l)(a) to include the real composition of Canadian society and to describe it in today's reality rather than in historical recollection of the past.
Another aspect which raises many questions is the reference to a distinct society. What on earth does "distinct society" mean? What is a "distinct society" in the Canadian context? I do not know. You must have been to Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker. It strikes me that that society is a distinct society, too, for different reasons. If you go over the mountains to the west you will find that British Columbians as well consider themselves to be a distinct society in sociological, collective, regional and geographical terms. One must then ask oneself whether New Brunswick is not also a distinct society. It recognizes bilingualism in its statutes and has a distinct character. The same can be said of Ontario. Before you know it, you will come to the conclusion that there are actually many distinct societies in this country. Therefore, why should we single one out in this process?
On the same subject I must ask what powers a province which has a distinct society within it would have. I do not know but it is evident that this distinction can lead to a number of powers which have not yet been examined or spelled out. For instance, does a provincial Government, which is a distinct society under the Constitution, have the power to override citizens' rights under the Charter? If it does, should it have those powers? We must clarify this question and many others which flow from the Accord.
As you must have noticed from newspaper articles, Mr. Speaker, there are people like Pierre-Marc Johnson who say that the constitutional Accord will spur sovereignty. The Minister of International Relations in Quebec, Gil Remillard, says that the Meech Lake Accord will confirm a special status for Quebec in international relations. Is that what was intended by the Premiers and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)? Is that what we are heading for? Is that what we want to have in this country? I do not see that that will be to the advantage of Canada or will make Canada stronger, as the Deputy Prime Minister said when he introduced his motion earlier this morning. This will not make Canada stronger at all.
In many passages the words of the Accord have been left vague. That is another aspect which needs attention. When there is vague terminology in any piece of legislation responsibility is shifted to judges to make political interpretations. Why should we saddle the judges with the task of second guessing what the politicians meant? That is not a good practice for writing legislation, particularly a piece of legislation of this importance. The consequences for the future of Canada of recognizing a distinct society are fundamental and have to be explored in detail and, in the long term, for the reasons 1 gave a moment ago.
With regard to other aspects of the legislation, I have grave reservations about how it affects immigrants. Immigrants can come into Canada under two sets of rules. Will an immigrant
Constitutional Accord
who has been pre-selected to go to Quebec have freedom of mobility? If, two or three days after arrival, an individual decides that he would like to move to another francophone region of the country for personal reasons, will he be bound to remain a permanent resident of the province for which he was selected?
What will happen to an immigrant who comes in under the other set of rules, chooses an English-speaking part of Canada, and decides after a short period of time to move to a Frenchspeaking part of Canada? Flow will the mobility rights of that individual be affected by the executive proposal in the Accord?
What happens to other rights which are presently in the Charter but are not referred to in the Accord? I am told by people with legal training that courts have a tendency to give precedence to parts of the Charter which may be singled out in the Constitution because of a convention that ordains that parts of the Charter which are not specified are not protected, are less protected. This is an item of extreme importance. Will the Charter be gutted by the fact that certain aspects of the Charter have not been mentioned or singled out in the Accord?
One must inevitably ask oneself whether the nation will be stronger as a result of the measures which the Government is proposing if the proposal is implemented and some of the consequences upon which I have elaborated come into being.
The point with which I will conclude has to do with appointments to the Senate and the Supreme Court. Will the nation become stronger through the appointment procedure put forth in the Meech Lake Accord? Would the nation be stronger if Senators and judges were appointed through a process that was initiated by the provinces? I can only state my opinion, that it has a very uneasy impact on me as a citizen because I still believe that while consultation is desirable, the shift, onus and initiative in appointments to national institutions should rest with the national Government and not be devolved or transferred to the components of Confederation.
I hold this belief for the very simple reason that there is an element of accountability. Inevitably, if one is appointed by the national Government, one's major responsibility and accountability will be to the totality of the nation rather than to a region in which one resides. This subtle shift in that accountability is one that I do not like.
Finally, the fact remains that we are witnessing in this Accord a gradual process of decentralization. There are appointments to the Senate, appointments to the Supreme Court, the distinct society and the spending power element which is very important. There is the immigration aspect as well. All of these are wrapped up into a unanimity clause. All of these small elements of decentralization combine to mean much decentralization.
This brings me to the important point concerning spending
powers. While Parliament was included in the first Accord, it
has been left out in the second Accord. The word "compatible"

June 12, 1987
Constitutional Accord
is so vague that no one really knows how to interpret it. No one knows according to that clause who is to set the national objectives.
One would hope that it would be the national Government, but it is not spelled out in that clause. It does not state clearly and unequivocally who is to set the national objectives. I would not want the Supreme Court of Canada to be faced decades from now with making a decision on this particular point.
Furthermore, I am not definite, but I have spoken to many people about the process of transferring powers which may make it impossible for the federal Government to stop payments to provinces which may decide in the future to introduce extra billing. Presently, the Government can stop payments, as we saw in a press release last week which stated that Ottawa refunded several million dollars to New Brunswick since it stopped extra billing. The federal Government must protect and retain that kind of power.
1 do not know what will happen to universality as a result of this particular clause, but 1 know that it is a clause that is vague and unsatisfactory. It puts to shame those in the House who have fought hard for universal programs, national programs and social security of the same quality and strength from coast to coast.
I want to conclude by putting forward a subamendment as a result of the very unsatisfactory answer given by the Deputy Prime Minister in reply to questions posed by the Hon. Member for St. Henri-Westmount when he asked what will happen in provinces where the provincial legislature will not hold public hearings in that province.
The Deputy Prime Minister sloughed the question off as a kind of superficial question that has no relevance to the debate today. 1 submit that the question is very relevant and important, in light of the fact that only last week Premier Getty of Alberta was reported to have said that there will be no public hearings in Alberta. 1 hope he will reverse his decision and hold public hearings, but in case some provinces do not do so in their respective areas, it seems that this committee or a subcommittee of the joint committee ought to hold public hearings in that particular province.
Therefore, I move the following subamendment:
That in provinces where the Legislature does not hold public hearings or has
not officially committed itself to hold public hearings, a sub-committee of the
Joint Committee be given powers to travel and hold public hearings in such
provinces.
There may be situations in which a province will not be able to hold hearings in the summer. Therefore, the subamendment is written in such a way as to take into account those provinces that will not hold public hearings in the summer months, but will make a public commitment to Canadians that their legislatures will hold public hearings. Thank you.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair will reserve for a few minutes on the admissibility of the amendment. In the meantime, we will proceed with the question and comment period.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for being able to raise so many important questions in such a short period of time.
At the very outset he questioned the motion on the basis of the time frame within which the public hearings are to be held and report back, as I recall, by September 14. He, like many of us, feels that that time frame is inadequate.
Having had considerable experience in committee work over the years, could he suggest what might be an adequate time frame, so that we do not simply leave it open-ended, but perhaps discuss among ourselves what time frame would be appropriate? Should we wait until we see the representations that people wish to make on the basis of the fundamental principle that as many Canadians as possible should be heard?
I am glad the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) is here to witness the concern of parliamentarians that this is too short a time frame. Again, I would urge the Deputy Prime Minister to support this subamendment which will ensure that people from coast to coast will have access to that committee, without having to travel across the country to Ottawa at their own expense.

Madam Speaker, I can understand the necessity and the desire of the Government to set a time frame. However, we should consider the length of time it takes us to examine other pieces of legislation. For example, we have been studying pornography for six months and we do not know how much longer we will be studying it. The House knows how long we could be studying capital punishment.
In light of that, on a fundamental piece of legislation like this, there ought to be an opportunity for ample hearings without such a limited time frame. I do not know whether a time frame should be set in this resolution, although I can understand the anxiety on the part of the Government to set a time frame. It has to be one that is practical. It seems to me, however, that as a minimum, there should be an examination of the Constitution, which is to last in its new proposed form- and I really hope there will be substantial fundamental amendments to the way it stands now-in order to give the public the time to absorb what is being proposed. We ourselves, who ought to understand it quickly and readily, have enormous difficulties. It should be given a time frame of six or even eight months and if, in the judgment of the members of the committee, that period of time turns out to be not adequate, then the time could be extended according to the best judgment of the members of that committee.
Since government Members would have the majority on the committee, they would be quite able to determine when that process ought to come to an end. It seems to me that it is not realistic and that it is-I hate to use such a heavy word but I cannot find a better one-undemocratic not to allow this examination. I know that the Deputy Prime Minister has his
June 12, 1987

heart in the right place and he is a democrat, but he does not seem to be consistent with the image 1 have of him when he imposes a time limit which is so restrictive.
1 am sure that if the Deputy Prime Minister were in the Opposition, he would make a more passionate speech, because he is more of a passionate speaker than 1 am myself, if not to keep it open-ended, at least to give it a breathing space, and three months is not enough.

Madam Speaker, I wish to support the sentiments expressed by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I want to say I also feel that the amount of time given to this committee is insufficient, given the importance of the questions with which we are dealing. After all, we are dealing with amendments to the Constitution of Canada. I think it is particularly important, in light of the fact we are really travelling in many respects through unchartered territory. There are provisions in the Constitution, as has been pointed out by the Hon. Member for Davenport, which are very ambiguous. I can refer to the opinion of a respected member of the legal profession, J. J. Robinette, who, a week or two ago said he felt that the courts and lawyers would have to deal with these ambiguities and suffer through the consequences of them for many, many years to come.
I think it is important to note that also because there were people who objected to the inclusion of a Charter of Rights in 1981 on the grounds that this would transfer power to the courts, that it would be the courts which would decide what the law of the land was, in the final analysis, and not the legislatures and the Parliament of Canada. I think there is an important distinction to be made between the Charter which was introduced in 1981 and the terms of the Meech Lake Agreement, and that is, that the rights set out in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms are rights which have already been subject to hundreds of years of interpretation, in many cases. It is true that the freedom of conscience and religion have to be refined from time to time in light of changing circumstances, mores, practices and habits in society. But can anyone deny that the freedom of conscience and religion are rights and freedoms which have formed the basis of legal decisions, interpretations and writings for hundreds of years? The same thing applies to the right to life, liberty and the security of the person. The same thing applies, although to a somewhat lesser extent, to the equality rights under Section 15 of the Charter.
Of course, the Charter contains minority language educational rights under Section 23, and those rights were framed fairly precisely. But even the provision such as the one, where numbers warrant, under which minority language groups would have the right to education in the minority language, was criticized precisely because it was said to be ambiguous. Nonetheless, in that case, there was some good evidence and a number of precedents to indicate what such a clause would mean in the final analysis.
Constitutional Accord
Therefore, I would submit that it is incorrect and illogical for those who are advocating changes to the Meech Lake Agreement, and some of the ambiguous changes, to say that this was the precise reason we were objecting to a Charter in the first place in 1980 or 1981. The rights and freedoms set out in the 1981 Charter are rights which were the subject of many years of interpretation, and I would suggest that it is entirely different now to propose concepts which are very ambiguous and many people do not know the meaning of them. Indeed, there are great differences of opinion as to the interpretation of certain clauses of this agreement.
Therefore, prudence dictates that this agreement, and certainly the ambiguous aspects of the agreement, be given full study by a committee of this House and by Parliament. If the Hon. Member for Davenport cares to respond, I would ask him if he does not agree with the distinction I am trying to make, namely that it is a far cry between the rights which were set out in the 1981 Charter and some of the very ambiguous provisions in the Meech Lake Agreement which, again, are subject to radically different interpretations?

In the limited time available, Madam Speaker, because the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) wants to participate in the debate, I would like to give a very brief answer, namely, that I do agree with the question which has been put to me.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Chair is now ready to rule on the subamendment which was submitted by the Hon. Member for Davenport.
The Chair will have to rule this subamendment out of order. We refer to the Fifth Edition of Beauchesne, Section 438(1) which states that if an amendment is intended to bring up matters foreign to the amendment, the Member should wait until the amendment is disposed of and move a new amendment.
The Chair feels that having hearings in provinces not officially committed to holding public hearings is bringing up a matter which is foreign to the amendment. Therefore, the subamendment is not admissible.
On a point of order, Madam Speaker, I would like to put forward a argument on this ruling if-

Then I am glad to challenge the Chair, if that is the procedure the Deputy Prime Minister wishes me to follow. I thought we could argue the ruling, but if it is the wish of this House that 1 challenge the Chair, I am prepared to challenge the Chair, and I will do so.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
As I said a few moments ago, the Chair feels that once the amendment now before the House has been disposed of, the Hon. Member could certainly propose, as an amendment, what he has

proposed to the House now. However, at this time, as a subamendment, the Chair feels it is not admissible. It is out of order.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-SELF-GOVERNMENT
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in order to recognize explicitly the right of Canada's aboriginal peoples to self-government, thereby making them partners in Confederation, and that this House further urges the Governments of Canada, the provinces and the territories to acknowledge that self-government requires a viable economic base, and calls upon these governments to constitutionally commit themselves to negotiate with the aboriginal peoples an equitable sharing of lands and resources.
He said: Madam Speaker, the motion now before the House follows rather closely the debate which has preceded it. The motion could very well have read: "That, in the opinion of this House, the recently agreed to Accord should be amended in order to recognize the right of Canada's aboriginal peoples to self-government". However, that is a fine point.
It is the Constitution Act, 1982, which the First Ministers' conferences on four different occasions have attempted but failed to amend.
In many parts of the world today very serious thought and consideration is being given to the problems and the rights of indigenous peoples who live in settled states or already-established nations. Frequently, the indigenous people to whom I refer live in underdeveloped or isolated parts of the particular country in question. Sometimes, even if they live where there is a population, that is, in an urban environment, they continue to live on the fringes of society. Recently, a very significant world report was presented on the environment and development. It is referred to as the Brundtland report. To its credit this report did not ignore the concerns and the problems of aboriginal peoples. For example, in reference to aboriginal peoples, it states in one of its sections:
Growing interaction with the larger world is increasing the vulnerability of these groups, since they are often left out of the processes of economic development. Social discrimination, cultural barriers, and the exclusion of these people from national political processes makes these groups vulnerable and subject to exploitation. Many groups become dispossessed and marginalized, and their traditional practices disappear. They become the victims of what could be described as cultural extinction.
I am sure, Madam Speaker, that in hearing that you must believe as I do that the people who put together the Brundtland report visited Canada or that they heard from expert witnesses from Canada.
Often for these very same people, no matter where they live-and they live in many parts of the world, not only in North America but also in Australia, the Amazon Basin, Central America and in the forests and hills of Asia-isolation has meant that few of them have shared in national economic and social development. That is reflected in the poor quality of life in many of their communities in terms of housing, economic development and opportunity, educational facilities, and even in terms of nutrition and health.
Strangely enough, if that situation were not serious enough, if a resource is discovered where they happen to live, if there is some opportunity to exploit the environment for material gain, then these people find themselves once again pushed aside and pushed out to make room for the developers. In the United Nations Organization today there is a Working Group on the Rights of Indigenous Populations. The group is chaired by a very remarkable woman, Dr. Erika Daes of Greece. She was an observer at the First Ministers' Conference that was held recently here in Ottawa which dealt with aboriginal rights in the Constitution.
Dr. Daes, after long and very careful research, has concluded the following about the right of self-determination. Selfdetermination is a term that goes back at least to the days of Woodrow Wilson, and perhaps even earlier than that. We certainly became familiar with the term on a world-wide basis at the time that the League of Nations was created. She said that the right of self-determination as we understand it over that period of time applies equally to indigenous peoples. She adds, however, that it does not mean the right to secession.
During the past 10 years Canada has given some very important, and I would say effective, leadership in recognizing aboriginal rights. It is now generally regarded that our federal system here in Canada is quite capable of accommodating native self-rule. I think most of us in the House realize that all that is really needed in order to accomplish this is some political will, a conviction that if we did so natural justice would be served.
In the Constitution of Canada today aboriginal rights are recognized in Section 35. That section states, among other things: "The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed." Did you know, Madam Speaker, that there are some people, who regard themselves as knowing something about the Constitution, who say that that is nothing but an empty box? They say that there is really nothing in it. Others, for whom I have a greater respect and whose views are more considered, believe that Section 35 is a full box of rights and that what we are undertaking to do at First Ministers' conferences is to draw from that full box of rights certain definitions, certain specific rights and, in particular, the right
June 12, 1987

of self-government or the right of self-determination within the Canadian Confederation.
This process of definition to which I have referred was, in fact, an obligation that was laid upon the Government of Canada and the provinces by the Constitution Act, 1982. Section 37 requires that there should be a number of these conferences in order to define with precision and exactness what are aboriginal rights. More and more the concentration has come to be the right of self-government.
My motion speaks to that very process, the process of recognizing the right to self-government within the Confederation of Canada or, to put it in another way, the process of completing the circle of Confederation. Until we recognize the rights of aboriginal people in Canada to control, to direct and to manage their own affairs within the Constitution and within our Confederation, we have a situation which is incomplete.
There have been a series of these conferences under the glare of television lights with a great deal of rhetoric exchanged among the Premiers, more than one Prime Minister, and the aboriginal leaders. So far we have not succeeded, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Elnatyshyn) have clearly indicated that we must not give up on this endeavour. I agree with both of them. The purpose of my motion is to say that this Elouse agrees with and supports the notion that the endeavour must be continued. Listen to what the Prime Minister said following the last conference:
I deeply regret that we did not succeed, but I give my hon. friend the assurance that we shall try again to make sure that justice comes about for the native peoples of Canada.
He went on that same day to say:
-we are still looking for a formula that will make it possible to enshrine the rights of aboriginal peoples in the Constitution of Canada. We did not succeed last week, but the federal Government's obligation is clear. I think the responsibility is equally shared by the provinces, and we intend to examine with them and the leaders of the various aboriginal groups the various alternatives available, in order to try and develop another formula that would meet with the requisite consent of various groups so that this right can finally be enshrined in the Canadian Constitution.
He also said:
I said with the greatest sadness that this was a moral obligation that has been unfulfilled by Canada, by the federal Government, by the provinces-
I quoted the Prime Minister because I want Members of the House to know that the motion I am putting forward today supports the desire by the Government of Canada, the Prime Minister, and a large number of Premiers, not enough but certain of them, to fulfil the unfulfilled obligation and complete the incomplete task. The motion now before us calls upon this House to lend its support to this endeavour which the Government of Canada has stated is a priority.
On May 28 in the House of Commons the Prime Minister, following the signing of the Meech Lake Accord and responding to questions about aboriginal people, said we have to:
The Constitution
... try to create a climate wherein it is generally recognized and accepted that a sense of justice and equity is required for the aboriginal peoples of Canada so that there can be a constitutional accord on this vital issue.
Through this motion I want to contribute positively to the favourable climate to which the Prime Minister referred. I have to say that that climate does now exist among a large number of Canadians. Some polling has been done to test their attitudes about recognizing aboriginal self-government. Some of our Premiers have been leading spokesmen on this yet unresolved issue. There are other Premiers, however, who remain apprehensive, fearful and hesitant. The Prime Minister said it is important that we try to create a climate so that the next time the First Ministers meet, a degree of success is attainable. Therefore, I submit that if today the House were to see its way clear to approve my motion, we would not be placing an obligation of any kind on the Government or on any province, but we would be helping to create the climate for which the Prime Minister has said there is a distinct need.
1 believe this House should be making some effort to help ensure success in the future. On June 8 the Minister of Justice said:
I share the disappointment. I think all Hon. Members of the House felt that we were unable to strike an arrangement on aboriginal constitutional amendments at the last First Ministers' meeting.
The Minister of Justice went on to say:
However, that was not the end of it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated at the conclusion of the First Ministers' meeting that it was not the end of it-
He said another meeting would depend upon an indication that progress could be made. I believe this House can play a role by approving this motion to help create the climate in which progress could be made. We are saying as Members of Parliament that we want and expect significant progress when the Prime Minister, the Premiers and the aboriginal leaders meet once again.
On that same day the Minister of Justice spoke of the need to maintain the priority to move toward the ultimate constitutionalization of the concept of self-government and aboriginal rights. That is the first time in my recollection that a senior member of the Government regarded this as a priority. They have always said it is important. They have always said it is a matter that has to be given full and undivided attention. Now the Minister of Justice has established it as a priority.
That being so, it is important that the House of Commons also express itself on this matter so that it remains a priority and in order to provide support to the active endeavours of the federal Government and encourage those provinces which still need further assurances.
Members who have taken the time to look at the motion will realize that I have gone a little further than to simply recognize within the Constitution the right of self-government. That is an essential starting point, but the motion goes on to talk about the need for a viable economic base for aboriginal selfgovernment. It also refers to the equitable sharing of lands and resources. In that regard I want to share with the House a

June 12, 1987
The Constitution
little more from the Brundtland report, the World Commission on Environment and Development. In one of its sections it
says:
Tribal and indigenous peoples will need special attention as the forces of economic development disrupt their traditional life-styles-life-styles that can offer modern societies many lessons in the management of resources in complex forest, mountain, and dryland ecosystems.
Some are threatened with virtual extinction by insensitive development over which they have no control. Their traditional rights should be recognized and they should be given a decisive voice in formulating policies about resource development in their areas.
I indicated earlier that this report has so much to say to Canada that one would have expected that some important witnesses from Canada had contributed to it. Sure enough that is the case. Louis Bruyere, President of the Native Council of Canada, is quoted in the report as follows:
Indigenous peoples are the base of what I guess could be called the environmental security system.
We are the gate-keepers of success or failure to husband our resources. For many of us, however, the last few centuries have meant a major loss of control over our lands and waters. We are still the first to know about changes in the environment, but we are now the last to be asked or consulted.
The most we have learned to expect is to be compensated, always too late and too little. We are seldom asked to help avoid the need for compensation by lending our expertise and our consent to development.
My motion would be incomplete if I did not talk about the need for sharing of land and resources and for an active say in the policies which lead to the development of those resources.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker,
I should like to address the second part of the motion of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) which "urges the Governments of Canada, the provinces, and the territories to acknowledge that self-government requires a viable economic base and calls upon these Governments to constitutionally commit themselves to negotiate with the aboriginal peoples an equitable sharing of lands and resources".
The recent First Ministers' Conference on aboriginal constitutional matters in March, 1987, did not result in an amendment. Nevertheless, my Government has taken a number of positive steps over the last several years which have resulted in significant actions in relation to lands and resources for aboriginal peoples.
The new comprehensive land claims policy announced by the Hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) in the House on December 18, 1986 was the culmination of a broad review.
This review was begun in 1985 when the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), established a task force under the able chairmanship of Murray Coolican which reported in March, 1986. This report and the subsequent consultations with aboriginal groups have been important to the development of this new policy.
Let me say at the very outset of my remarks that the Government of Canada, by bringing forward this new policy, has affirmed that the resolution of claims arising from aboriginal title is a major priority, a priority shared with Canada's aboriginal peoples. My Government is committed to the settlement of these claims by direct negotiations.
Some highlights of these changes to the comprehensive claims policy are directly related to aboriginal self-government and the equitable sharing of land and resources.
The federal Government acknowledges that self-government and claims policies are related. The management of settlement benefits and the administration of lands and resources are governmental matters. Changes to claims policy will allow for the negotiation of a broader range of self-government matters concerned with the authority and control over aboriginal lands.
Self-government is often spoken of as the exercise by a community of responsibility for its own members and of authority over the affairs of the community. Another aspect to self-government affecting aboriginal groups is participation in the exercise of powers within the broader framework of public government. This aspect sets self-government in the claims process somewhat outside the community-based self-government negotiations. As a result of the changes in claims policy, it is expected that settlements will recognize a specific aboriginal managerial interest in relation to a number of environmental matters such as water, land use, and wildlife management.
It is not proper, on the one hand, to recognize special harvesting rights for an aboriginal group and, on the other hand, to exclude the harvesters of the resources affected from responsibility for their management.
Under the policy, therefore, aboriginal groups will be able to negotiate membership on a variety of management boards and other agencies with decision-making powers, as well as representation on advisory committees as was possible under the previous policy.
These arrangements must not only acknowledge that public governments have a responsibility to protect the interests of all users of resources, to ensure resource conservation, to respect international agreements, and to manage renewable resources within their jurisdiction. However, such arrangements will also recognize aboriginal groups as having a unique interest in the governance of the resources.
In speaking of environmental and renewable resources, 1 include marine areas traditionally and currently utilized by aboriginal groups. This is an important matter which has required clarification. The Inuit, in particular, have been concerned that much of their hunting has been traditionally carried out on what is called land-fast sea ice in certain seasons and by boat at other times. Similarly, Indian groups in coastal areas have traditionally relied heavily upon the harvesting of marine resources.
June 12, 1987

The federal Government is now prepared, in recognition of this use, to negotiate with aboriginal groups matters relating to the harvesting and management of renewable resources in marine areas, not only on land.
My remarks thus far have demonstrated my Government's firm position on the matters of lands, resources, and selfgovernment which have been raised in the Hon. Member's motion. In addition, the motion made reference to "a viable economic base" for aboriginal self-government.
The changes to the claims policy relating to economic benefits have been of particular importance to aboriginal groups. Under the former policy, sub-surface land rights in defined areas could be granted to aboriginal groups, in some instances in order to avoid land use conflicts in key areas and, in other instances, as a means to provide aboriginal people with the opportunity to obtain revenue from the development of such sub-surface resources. This option will continue to be available to claimant groups.
In addition, and under the new policy, my Government is prepared to provide to aboriginal groups a percentage of Crown royalties derived from the extraction of resources in the entire settlement area. I would stress that this option will include not only royalties from sub-surface resources but will also include non-renewable resources extracted from offshore areas which form part of the claims settlement area.
It is my belief that this option will be of special interest to aboriginal groups, as it will assist in providing the tangible means to build the economy not only of the particular aboriginal groups but of Canada as a whole. This policy is proof of our commitment to equitable sharing and our support for a viable economic basis.
My Government believes that commitments are empty without action. The policies of my Government go beyond mere commitments and will result in concrete solutions to the very real economic issues the Hon. Member has raised in his motion. I am optimistic that over the next several months we will begin to see meaningful results flowing from these policy changes.
The agreements resulting from comprehensive claims settlements will be entrenched in the Constitution as existing treaty rights, as provided in Section 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982. The key points I would emphasize are referred to in the motion. My Government is committed to negotiate and to protect constitutionally agreements concluded pursuant to negotiations.
In closing, I want to say that it was an honour for me to speak on the Hon. Member's motion today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ABORIGINAL PEOPLES-SELF-GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to express appreciation to the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for bringing forward this very important motion. It is important, not because we need to hear more speeches on the question of aboriginal self-government, but because it gives the House an
The Constitution
opportunity to express its will and intention with regard to aboriginal self-government. In part the motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Act, 1982, should be amended in order to recognize explicitly the right of Canada's aboriginal peoples to self-government-
This position is supported in principle by all three Parties and has been for some time, at least since 1983 when the report on Indian self-government was tabled in the House of Commons by the Hon. Member who introduced the motion.
As I said, the report was endorsed by all three Parties in the House. It was the result of travel across Canada by a committee to hear the considered opinion of aboriginal leaders. Then we sat down and thought about it very seriously among ourselves and expressed different partisan points of view. We came to a consensus that what we needed was a fundamental change in the relationship between Canada and its aboriginal peoples, and that the basis for that change should be a recognition of the rights of these people to govern themselves, a right which they had in the past, a right which they never surrendered, and a right which needs to be empowered so that it can become meaningful in the last half of the 20th century. This is not simply a frill, not simply a constitutional nicety, or something that would be desirable if all other things were equal. This is something that is basic to the future of the aboriginal peoples as a people. Without that kind of provision, aboriginal peoples face a form of systemic discrimination, which is unacceptable in Canada in 1987. I want to give just one example which is taken from yesterday's paper. This article reads:
Natives are denied parole more often than non-natives, in part because of a lack of parole supervisors in rural areas, says a spokesman for the National Parole Board. In Alberta, from January 1, 1979, to December 31, 1985, full parole was granted to 43 per cent of non-natives, but to only 20 per cent of natives, board member Ken Howland said Tuesday.
Here we have a situation where our Government, which is supposed to be looking after the interests of aboriginal peoples, does not provide the kinds of facilities in rural areas which allows Indian prisoners to have the right of parole in the same way that non-native prisoners would have. That is a form of systemic discrimination which could be overcome if there were a form of self-government in place whereby Indian people would be responsible for that kind of service themselves.
As long as we maintain that, we will continue to have native people in our prisons. We will continue to have discrimination showing up in all kinds of ways, in health, education, job opportunities and so on. This, I want to emphasize, is not a frill. It is not something that we can take or leave. It is absolutely essential if we want to see basic justice for the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
Over the past few weeks there has been a great deal of congratulation over the very significant achievement reached in the Meech Lake Accord between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the First Ministers. It is significant because it overcomes a very key flaw in the 1982 Constitutional Accord

June 12, 1987
The Constitution
where nine provinces and the Government of Canada agreed on certain constitutional changes that the Government of Quebec was not able to agree to. In a sense, Quebec was left out even though legally it was still part of the Canadian Confederation.
The significant thing about this constitutional Accord is that now for the first time a democratically elected Government of Quebec is able to sign that paper and say, "Yes, we are part of the Canadian Confederation", a very important and significant achievement. Some people question whether or not the price is too high. Every concerned Canadian recognizes the importance of Quebec being a part of that Accord. It was possible because there was a commitment across Canada to seeing that happen. There was a commitment on the part of the Prime Minister and on the part of a significant number of the provincial Premiers so that other Premiers were carried along. Bill Vander Zalm a few years ago said he would be just as happy if Quebec separated because then he would not need to read French on his corn flakes box. He is rather a flaky Premier, Madam Speaker.
